passage:
Looking back at second year, I can see exactly what I was doing. My marks in two papers dropped, and the hostel fee reminder came three times. Each time I thought, "It'll sort itself out. Something will turn up." When the student counsellor emailed, I archived it without opening it. Not looking felt strangely calm.
My roommate Divyansh asked once whether I'd paid the fee. I changed the subject to the cricket match.
Then the notice went up: fees unpaid by Friday meant no hall ticket. My stomach dropped. On Thursday I finally opened that email, sat in the counsellor's office, and learnt about an instalment option I could have known about weeks earlier.
— Binita

qa.q: What did Binita do with the counsellor's email?
qa.a: Archived it without opening it.

qa.q: Why did not looking feel strangely calm to Binita?
qa.a: Avoiding the email and reminders kept the dread at a distance, so it felt calmer than facing falling marks and an unpaid fee.

qa.q: What could Binita have done at the first fee reminder instead?
qa.a: Opening the counsellor's email or asking the office straight away could have turned up the instalment option weeks earlier, with far less panic.

qa.q: What might Divyansh have sensed when Binita changed the subject?
qa.a: Divyansh may have sensed something was wrong with the fee and felt unsure whether to push or let it go.

grounding: A student looks back on dodging falling marks, fee reminders and the counsellor's email until a hall-ticket deadline forced action.

passage:
Student support note: Pallavi, B.Com second year
I emailed Pallavi on 3 and 17 September after her attendance and internal marks dropped. No reply. A friend of hers told me Pallavi kept saying, "It'll sort itself out, I'm just tired."
On 1 October the accounts office flagged unpaid fees; exam registration closes on the 10th. Today, the 8th, Pallavi came in holding the office printout. She said she had seen my emails in her inbox and couldn't make herself click them.
I didn't lecture. We made three calls together: the accounts office, her class mentor, and her father. By the end she was breathing more easily.
Next: weekly check-in on Mondays.
— Himani

qa.q: When did the accounts office flag Pallavi's unpaid fees?
qa.a: On 1 October.

qa.q: Why couldn't Pallavi make herself click the emails?
qa.a: Opening them would have made the falling marks and fees real, and not looking kept the dread down until the deadline came close.

qa.q: What choice by Himani helped once Pallavi came in?
qa.a: Himani skipped the lecture and made the three calls alongside her, turning a frightening pile into a few concrete steps.

qa.q: How might Pallavi's friend have felt hearing 'It'll sort itself out'?
qa.a: The friend may have been worried but unsure what to do, sensing that things weren't really fine.

grounding: A support officer's note records a student ignoring falling marks, unpaid fees and emails until the registration deadline brought her in.

12 March, 11 pm
Didn't open the portal again today. I know the mid-sem marks are up. I know they're low; Sarika checked hers and went quiet when she looked at me. Fee reminder number four is sitting unread too.
Told myself: next week things will calm down and I'll deal with it then. Somehow that thought makes my shoulders drop, even though nothing has changed.
And the counsellor's email. Subject line: "Checking in." Skipped it. Watched three episodes of a baking show instead.
Sarika just told me the fee window closes Friday. Friday. That's three days away.
Okay. Tomorrow I open the portal. Maybe the email too.
— Lavanya

qa.q: What was the subject line of the counsellor's email?
qa.a: "Checking in."

qa.q: Why does the thought 'next week things will calm down' make Lavanya's shoulders drop?
qa.a: Putting it off to next week brings instant relief from the dread, even though the marks and fees haven't changed at all.

qa.q: What would be a workable first step for Lavanya tomorrow?

qa.q: What might Sarika feel when she tells Lavanya the fee window closes Friday?
qa.a: Sarika is probably worried for Lavanya and may have been waiting for the right moment to say it.

grounding: A student's diary shows unopened marks, fee reminders and a skipped counsellor email until a Friday deadline starts to force the issue.

passage: In the girls' hostel of the small college in Hassan, Indu, nineteen, had tucked the counsellor's letter inside her economics book, unopened. Her internal marks had slid from sixties to thirties. The hostel fee slip was two months old. "It'll sort itself out," she told her roommate Payal, and went to the temple fair with the juniors every evening that week, laughing a little too loudly. Payal noticed she'd stopped studying at night and slept badly. On Monday morning a notice went up outside the office: students with unpaid fees would not get exam hall tickets after Wednesday. Indu's name was on it. She stood staring for a long time. Then she went back to the room, opened the economics book, and read the counsellor's letter for the first time. "Payal," she said quietly, "will you come with me?"

qa.q: Where had Indu tucked the counsellor's letter?
qa.a: Inside her economics book, unopened.

qa.q: Why did Indu go to the temple fair every evening and laugh a little too loudly?
qa.a: Keeping busy and cheerful helped her push away the dread about her marks and fees, so she didn't have to look at them.

qa.q: What forced Indu to act, and what could have helped earlier?
qa.a: The notice with her name forced her; reading the counsellor's letter when it came, or telling Payal sooner, could have helped before it became urgent.

qa.q: How might Payal have seen Indu during that week?
qa.a: Payal noticed the stopped studying and poor sleep, and was probably worried but unsure how to help until Indu asked.

passage: Pallavi walked down the college corridor in Dehradun past the counsellor's office without looking at the door. Her second-semester marks had dropped from firsts to barely passing. The fees office had sent two reminders. There was also an email from the student counsellor, subject line "Checking in", sitting unread for three weeks. "It'll sort itself out," she told Sachin when he asked. "Papa will send the money soon. The marks were just a bad term." Sachin had noticed she'd stopped coming to morning lectures. On Friday a printed notice went up on the board: students with unpaid fees could not sit the exams on the fifteenth. Pallavi's name was on it. She stood staring at it for a long time. Then Sachin walked her to the counsellor's office.

passage: Kiran, you keep asking why I was so strange last year, so here's the honest version from me, Irfan. Second year, my marks started falling. First a C, then two Ds. The fees were late too. Abbu's business had a bad year. Every time I thought about it, my stomach turned over, so I stopped thinking about it. I'd say, "It'll work out." The college counsellor sent me an email. I saw the subject, "Let's talk", and archived it without reading. I did that four times. I actually got good at not looking. Then a notice came: pay by the thirtieth or no exam hall ticket. That was the day I finally walked into the counsellor's office, shaking. She helped me meet the fees officer, who explained the options. If I'd opened that first email, I'd have had two months, not two weeks.

qa.q: How many times did Irfan archive the counsellor's emails?
qa.a: Four times.

qa.q: Why did Irfan get good at not looking?
qa.a: Irfan felt dread and a turning stomach whenever the marks and fees came to mind, so avoiding them felt like relief in the moment.

qa.q: What does Irfan wish had been done differently?
qa.a: Opening the counsellor's first email, which would have given two months to sort things out instead of two weeks.

qa.q: How might the counsellor have seen the unanswered emails?
qa.a: The counsellor was probably concerned, reaching out repeatedly because falling marks and late fees suggested a student in trouble.

Abhinav, you're not opening the college emails? Let your Jeevan chacha tell you what I did at twenty.

My marks were falling. I owed hostel fees. Every morning I told myself, "It'll sort itself out." The warden left notes. I tore them up.

I thought if I didn't look, it wasn't real. But I slept badly and snapped at everyone.

Then one morning, a letter said I couldn't sit exams unless fees were paid in a week. My hands shook.

I went to the college counsellor that day. She helped me talk to the fees office and my father. We sorted it out, but it was much harder than if I'd gone months earlier.

Dread, Abhinav, grows in the dark. Open the emails.

passage:
Yamini had one day left. Her college had sent five emails about her unpaid fees and falling attendance. She'd opened none of them. Her phone had cracked last week, and she used it as an excuse: "I can't read emails properly."

Her roommate Swati found her lying on the bed at noon, staring at the ceiling.

"You look sick."

"I'm fine. It'll sort itself out."

Swati held up her own phone. "The counsellor emailed me asking if you're okay. The deadline's tomorrow."

Yamini's stomach dropped. She sat up.

"I'll come with you," Swati said. "Now."

They walked to the counsellor's office that afternoon. Yamini's hands shook, but she went in.

qa.q: How many emails had Yamini's college sent?
qa.a: Five emails.

qa.q: Why did Yamini keep saying "It'll sort itself out"?
qa.a: She felt dread and avoided looking, hoping the problems would disappear if she didn't face them.

qa.q: What did Swati do that finally got Yamini moving?
qa.a: She told Yamini about the counsellor's email and the deadline, and went with her to the office right away.

qa.q: How might Swati feel when she sees Yamini staring at the ceiling?
qa.a: Swati probably feels worried and determined to help her friend.

grounding: Under a deadline, a student who ignored emails about fees and attendance is forced to face them with a friend's help.

Harish sat on his bed with the notice for a long time. Afreen found him there. "Let's go to the counsellor. Now. I'll come with you."

passage: Last year I got very good at not looking. My marks were slipping, and a fee instalment was overdue because I had lost a part-time job and hadn't told my parents. The college counsellor, Arohi ma'am, emailed me twice. I archived both without reading them. I told myself it would sort itself out, that next month would be different. It wasn't dread exactly; it was more like a fog I kept walking around. Then the exam form portal locked me out: "Dues pending." Three days to the deadline. That's when I finally opened her emails. She could help arrange a payment plan and study support. I sat in her office that afternoon, embarrassed. I'm Eshaan, and now I open hard emails on the day they arrive.

qa.q: What message did the exam form portal show?
qa.a: "Dues pending."

qa.q: How does Eshaan describe the feeling of not looking?
qa.a: Like a fog Eshaan kept walking around: a dread kept at bay by avoidance, followed by embarrassment when finally facing it.

qa.q: What changed Eshaan's approach, and what habit came from it?
qa.a: The locked portal forced it; Eshaan met the counsellor that afternoon and now opens hard emails the day they arrive.

qa.q: How might Arohi ma'am have felt when Eshaan finally came?
qa.a: Relieved and ready to help, since she had been trying to reach Eshaan with support.

passage:
Hostel warden's log, Block C, the week the winter fog set in.
Monday: Madhav came to my desk worried about his roommate. Harsha had three unopened letters from the accounts office and had failed two internal tests. When I asked Harsha, he laughed. "It'll sort itself out. First-term results are always weird."
Wednesday: The counsellor told me Harsha had not answered her two emails. At breakfast I saw him scroll straight past them.
Friday: The accounts office pinned the final date for fees on the notice board: next Tuesday. Harsha stood reading it for a long time, then knocked on my door, pale. I walked him to the counsellor's room that afternoon and asked someone from accounts to join. Madhav waited outside with two cups of tea.

qa.q: What did the accounts office pin on the notice board?
qa.a: The final date for fees: next Tuesday.

qa.q: Why did Harsha laugh and say it would sort itself out?
qa.a: He felt dread about the fees and marks, and not looking kept that fear at a distance, so ignoring the letters felt easier than opening them.

qa.q: What could have helped Harsha sooner?
qa.a: Opening one letter with Madhav or the warden early and replying to the counsellor would have let him get help before the deadline forced it.
